label: Spaces of Constant Curvature
notes: This opening frame sets the agenda for printed pages 155 to 190: classify the manifolds whose sectional curvature is one fixed constant. We will meet the three simply connected models, state Cartan's rigidity theorem, and build complete space forms as discrete quotients.

label: Constant Sectional Curvature
notes: Here we make the hypothesis precise. Constant curvature requires the sectional curvature of every two-plane, at every point, to equal the same scalar K. Emphasize that this independence from plane and base point is the strongest curvature condition short of flatness.

label: The Curvature Tensor Formula
notes: This slide delivers the central algebraic fact: under constant curvature the Riemann tensor reduces to K times the metric combination of inner products. Stress that the metric and the single number K now reconstruct every curvature component without any extra data.

label: Three Model Geometries
notes: We organize the whole chapter by the sign of K. Positive gives the round sphere, zero gives Euclidean space, and negative gives hyperbolic space. Preview how geodesics and parallels differ across the three simply connected model geometries shown side by side.

label: The Sphere: K = 1
notes: Focus on the sphere as the positive-curvature prototype. Geodesics are great circles, any two meet, so parallel lines fail to exist. The space is compact with bounded diameter, the canonical example of a closed finite-volume space form.

label: Euclidean Space: K = 0
notes: Treat flat space as the borderline model where the Riemann tensor vanishes identically. Geodesics are straight lines and the classical parallel postulate holds, with exactly one parallel through an external point. It is the unique simply connected zero-curvature model.

label: Hyperbolic Space: K = -1
notes: Introduce hyperbolic space through the Poincare disk model. Geodesics are diameters and circular arcs orthogonal to the boundary, and infinitely many disjoint geodesics pass through a point off a given line, the dramatic failure of the parallel postulate.

label: Geodesic Triangle Angle Sums
notes: Connect curvature to a measurable invariant: the angle sum of a geodesic triangle. Positive curvature produces excess above pi, flat space gives exactly pi, and negative curvature gives a defect below pi, all governed by the integral of K over the triangle.

label: Cartan's Determination Theorem
notes: State Cartan's theorem: spaces of equal constant curvature are locally isometric. The proof composes the inverse exponential map, a linear isometry of tangent spaces, and the target exponential map, showing the three models exhaust every local possibility up to isometry.

label: Space Forms as Quotients
notes: Move from local to global. Any complete constant-curvature manifold has one of the three models as universal cover and equals that cover modulo a discrete group of isometries acting freely and properly discontinuously, with the group isomorphic to the fundamental group.

label: Discrete Isometry Groups
notes: Survey the groups that realize space forms. Translation lattices on Euclidean space build flat tori, finite fixed-point-free rotation groups on the sphere build lens spaces, and Fuchsian groups on the hyperbolic plane build higher-genus surfaces, each acting freely to preserve manifold structure.

label: Recap and Synthesis
notes: Summarize the chapter as four linked ideas: the single curvature tensor formula, the three models indexed by the sign of K, Cartan rigidity giving local isometry, and discrete quotients giving the global classification. These results seed the comparison theorems of later chapters.
